J1_line_asserts_challenged_proposition.justification: The response challenges "S can be embedded via s_alpha to alpha into the ordinal beta which is the union of all such alpha." First-choice line 28 asserts exactly that: "Now, we can impose a well-ordering on $S$ by embedding it via $s_\alpha \to \alpha$ into the ordinal $\beta = \ds {\bigcup_{s_\alpha \mathop \in S} \alpha}$ and using the well-ordering of $\beta$." Active assumptions: S is an arbitrary set (line 1, and P3 claims every set), c is a choice function on the non-empty subsets of S (line 5), the s_alpha are produced by the recursion of lines 15-24, and the process has stopped (lines 21, 26).

J2_evidence_specified.justification: A specific instance with the resulting ordinal computed and the failure named: "If S is a singleton, the only index used is alpha = 0, making beta = 0, but a non-empty set cannot be embedded into the empty set." The set, the index set, the value of beta and the reason no embedding exists are all given.

J3_evidence_check.justification: Exact computation with von Neumann ordinals represented literally as sets, script kept. For a singleton S = {x}: line 15 gives s_0 = c(S) = x, then S minus {s_0} is empty so line 21 stops the recursion, hence the only index used is alpha = 0. Line 28's beta is then the set-theoretic union of {0}, which the script computes to be the empty set, i.e. the ordinal 0; and 0 is not an element of 0, so the map s_alpha |-> alpha does not take S into beta, and since S is non-empty while beta is empty no injection S -> beta exists at all. So line 28's assertion fails for an admissible S (the theorem is asserted for every set), which refutes the line as written. The script also shows the same failure for every finite non-empty size (beta comes out as n-1 while the indices run to n-1), and records the contrasting case: when the set of indices has no largest element, e.g. a countably infinite S with indices 0,1,2,..., the union is omega and does contain every index -- so the defect is precisely that a union rather than a supremum of successors was taken.

J4_consequence_overreach.justification: The saved response is only the JSON object with one candidate label, the challenged claim and the counterexample. It asserts no further consequence -- nothing about Zermelo's Well-Ordering Theorem itself, the Axiom of Choice or the earlier steps -- so there is no stated consequence that could overreach.

notes: For a second reader: the defect is an off-by-one in the choice of target ordinal (union of the indices instead of the least ordinal strictly above them), and it bites exactly when the set of indices used has a largest element, which includes every finite non-empty S. A reader inclined to read the union charitably as 'the least ordinal not used' would find nothing wrong, but as written the formula is the union, and the singleton makes it the empty set. Note also that the more commonly criticised step in this proof is line 26 ('The process eventually stops, else we have defined bijections between subsets of S and arbitrarily large ordinals'), which is where the substantive appeal to replacement/Hartogs hides; the response did not go there, and its line-28 objection stands on its own.
